title: LEVITICUS HAD TO TELL ISRAEL NOT TO SLEEP WITH A BROTHER’S WIFE
paragraphs: LEVITICUS HAD TO TELL ISRAEL NOT TO SLEEP WITH A BROTHER’S WIFE

And thousands of years later, one fearless preacher confronted a king over the same command—and lost his head. But beneath this disturbing law is something far more personal: what happens when desire starts demanding permission to cross a boundary God has already drawn?
There are verses in the Bible we underline.
There are verses we put on coffee mugs.
There are verses we whisper beside hospital beds, print on T-shirts, frame above fireplaces, and send to friends when life is falling apart.
And then there is Leviticus 18:16.
A verse almost nobody puts on a coffee mug.
In Hebrew it reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָחִיךָ הִוא
ʿErwat ʾeshet-ʾaḥikha lo tegalleh; ʿerwat ʾaḥikha hi.
Literally, with the Hebrew idiom preserved:
“The nakedness of your brother’s wife you shall not uncover; it is your brother’s nakedness.”
That language sounds strange to modern ears.
But “uncover nakedness” is a recurring Hebrew expression in Leviticus 18 describing prohibited sexual relations.
So strip away the distance of three thousand years and hear what God was actually telling Israel:
There are sexual boundaries you do not cross.
Including this one.
Your brother’s wife is not yours to take.
And perhaps the uncomfortable question is not merely, “Why did God have to command this?”
Perhaps the more frightening question is:
Why does God have to command human beings not to do so many things that should already feel unthinkable?
Because Scripture does not flatter us.
The Bible does not present humanity as basically pure people occasionally making unfortunate mistakes.
It tells a much darker story.
And then it tells a much better one.
We are creatures capable of taking something beautiful that God created and twisting it around ourselves.
Love.
Sex.
Marriage.
Power.
Family.
Desire.
Even religion.
Give the human heart something good, and sin will eventually whisper:
What if you used it your way instead of God's?
That is why Leviticus 18 matters far beyond one ancient prohibition.
It is holding up a mirror.
God had delivered Israel from Egypt, and now He was teaching a redeemed people that deliverance was supposed to change how they lived.
They were not to imitate the sexual practices of the nations around them.
They belonged to Yahweh.
And belonging to God meant that even their most private desires were not beyond His authority.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because we love a Jesus who enters our suffering.
We are less comfortable with a Jesus who enters our bedroom.
We love a God who heals our wounds.
We become nervous when that same God challenges our appetites.
We celebrate grace when grace means forgiveness.
We sometimes resist grace when grace means transformation.
But biblical grace never says:
“Keep whatever is destroying you.”
Grace says:
“Come out of the grave.”
Leviticus returns to the brother’s-wife prohibition later with even stronger language:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִקַּח אֶת־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו נִדָּה הִוא
Weʾish ʾasher-yiqqaḥ ʾet-ʾeshet ʾaḥiw, niddah hi...
Leviticus 20:21 condemns a man taking his brother’s wife and describes the act as a violation of his brother’s nakedness.
But careful Bible reading matters here.
This should not be carelessly turned into the claim that Scripture prohibited every possible union between a man and his brother’s widow under every circumstance.

Deuteronomy 25:5–10 gives Israel a specific provision commonly called levirate marriage: when brothers lived together and one died without a son, the surviving brother had a covenant responsibility concerning his deceased brother’s widow and family line.
That is not a contradiction we need to hide.
Context matters.
Leviticus is prohibiting illicit sexual appropriation.
Deuteronomy addresses a particular situation involving a deceased brother, preservation of his family line, and responsibility toward his widow.
Scripture deserves more than slogans.
It deserves to be read carefully enough that we do not make God say something He did not say.
And then centuries passed.
Empires rose.
Empires collapsed.
Israel's kings became dust.
The prophets died.
And eventually another ruler decided he wanted his brother’s wife.
His name was Herod Antipas.
Her name was Herodias.
And standing between royal desire and biblical truth was a wilderness preacher who apparently had not learned the modern art of making conviction marketable.
John the Baptist.
Imagine the scene.
Herod had political authority.
John had camel's hair.
Herod had soldiers.
John had a voice.
Herod could imprison John.
John could tell Herod the truth.
And he did.
The Gospel records the accusation with terrifying simplicity:
Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.
Ouk exestin soi echein tēn gynaika tou adelphou sou.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
No sophisticated rebranding.
No attempt to make sin sound respectable because the sinner was powerful.
John looked toward a ruler who could destroy him and essentially said:
God's boundary still stands.
And eventually John's head was carried into a banquet.
Think about that.
A command from Leviticus became part of the reason a prophet lost his life.
John could have remained silent.
He could have preached something safer.
He could have told Herod that God loved him without ever explaining that the love of God called him to repentance.
He could have protected his platform.
Protected his influence.
Protected his neck.
But John understood something much of modern Christianity desperately needs to recover:
Love does not become more loving by hiding the truth that could lead someone to repentance.
Yet there is another danger here.
A religious person can read an article about sexual sin and immediately begin thinking about everybody else's bedroom.
Herod.
Herodias.
That relative.
That celebrity.
That friend.
That person at church.
Anybody...
except the person reading.
So before you use Leviticus as binoculars to inspect somebody else's sin, use it as a mirror.
Maybe you have never touched your brother's wife.
But perhaps you have crossed another boundary while telling yourself it was different because your feelings were sincere.
Perhaps nobody knows what is on your phone after midnight.
Perhaps your spouse believes you are faithful because you have carefully narrowed the definition of unfaithfulness.
Perhaps there is a conversation you delete.
A relationship you keep hidden.
A fantasy you repeatedly feed.
A pornography history nobody sees.
A flirtation you call harmless.
An emotional affair you insist is only friendship.
A secret account.
A second life.
Or perhaps sexual sin is not your battlefield at all.
Perhaps your hidden room contains bitterness.
Envy.
Pride.
Greed.
Dishonesty.
Resentment.
Self-righteousness.
A wound you have turned into permission to wound others.
The details change.
The ancient whisper does not.
Did God really say you cannot have this?
That whisper is older than Leviticus.
Older than Israel.
Older than Egypt.
It was already crawling through Eden.
The serpent did not begin by forcing Eve to eat.
He began by making God's boundary seem suspicious.
That is still how temptation works.
First the boundary feels restrictive.
Then crossing it feels reasonable.
Then repeating it feels normal.
Then hiding it feels necessary.
Then defending it feels personal.
Eventually repentance feels like an attack on your identity because you have lived beside the sin so long that you no longer know where it ends and you begin.
And that is exactly where Jesus becomes more beautiful than we expected.
Because Christ did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came looking for sinners.
People with histories.
People with stains.
People with appetites they could not control.
People who had crossed boundaries.
People who had been sexually broken.
People who had broken others.
Religious hypocrites.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Thieves.
The ashamed.
The self-righteous.
The ruined.
Us.
The Gospel is not the announcement that sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin matters so much that the Son of God went to Calvary.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that sinners are beyond recovery.
Look at the cross again.
God loved sinners so deeply that Christ went there willingly.
That tension is Christianity.
Your sin is worse than your excuses have admitted, and Christ's mercy is greater than your shame has imagined.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by entering the scandal with nail-scarred hands.
He does not rename darkness as light.
He brings light into darkness.
He does not call bondage freedom.
He breaks chains.
He does not tell the guilty person, “There was never anything to forgive.”
He offers something infinitely better:
real forgiveness.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the doorway through which the person who is finished hiding finally walks toward home.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It speaks of turning, reconsidering, changing one's mind in a way that redirects life toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns.
Toward Christ.
Toward truth.
Toward obedience.
Toward the Father.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years believing that if Christians knew what happened, they would never look at you the same way.
Maybe you crossed sexual boundaries.
Maybe somebody crossed yours.
Those are not morally identical things, and they should never be treated as though they are.
If you were sexually abused, coerced, exploited, or violated, another person's sin against you is not transformed into your guilt simply because it involved your body.
Hear that clearly.
But if you willingly sinned...
hear this just as clearly:
You do not have to spend the rest of your life hiding either.
Confession may be painful.
Consequences may remain.
Trust may take time to rebuild.
Repentance may require difficult changes.
Grace does not magically erase every earthly consequence of our choices.
But Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
The blood shed at Calvary was not reserved for people with presentable testimonies.
There are no presentable testimonies.
There are only different versions of:
I needed mercy.
Maybe that is why this obscure command in Leviticus can hit so hard.
It begins with another man's wife.
It ends with your heart.
What boundary have you been negotiating with God about?
What have you renamed so you would not have to repent of it?
What would terrify you if it appeared publicly tonight?
What relationship are you protecting more fiercely than your obedience to Christ?
What secret has begun demanding more and more of you?
And how long are you planning to hide?
Because sin makes extraordinary promises.
Then sends devastating invoices.
It promises pleasure and collects peace.
Promises intimacy and collects integrity.
Promises freedom and collects your ability to look people in the eyes.
Promises secrecy and slowly builds a prison.
Then Jesus stands outside the cell.
Not pretending there are no bars.
Not pretending you did not walk inside.
But holding the key.
There is a reason 1 John 1:9 has rescued so many trembling believers: when we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive and cleanse.
Not because confession purchases mercy.
Because Christ already purchased redemption.
And there is a reason Romans 8:1 sounds almost impossible to people who finally understand their guilt:
There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not reduced condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
Not condemnation waiting until God gets tired of you.
No condemnation.
For whom?
Those in Christ Jesus.
That is the center.
Not moral self-improvement.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
Christ.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who welcomed sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who told the truth about sin without becoming cruel to sinners.
The One who carried a cross through Jerusalem.
The One whose hands were pierced.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who still saves.
Maybe you clicked because the title sounded scandalous.
Good.
Now let the scandal lead you to grace.
Because the greatest scandal in this story is not that ancient Israel needed laws governing sexual boundaries.
The greatest scandal is that a holy God knew exactly what humanity would become...
and still chose redemption.
He knew Peter would deny.
He knew Thomas would doubt.
He knew His disciples would scatter.
He knew what you would do.
He knew what I would do.
And Christ still walked toward Golgotha.
That does not give us permission to sin.
It destroys the excuse that says repentance is pointless because we have sinned too much.
So stop bargaining.
Stop editing the story.
Stop calling chains jewelry.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
If restitution is needed, pursue it wisely.
If accountability is needed, seek it.
If a relationship must end because maintaining it requires continuing sin, obedience may hurt—but Christ is worth more than the thing you are afraid to surrender.
If you have fallen again after promising God you never would, do not turn another failure into an excuse for another year of hiding.
Run to Christ.
Not away from Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Get up.
Walk again.
And when Satan whispers, “Look what you did,” learn to answer by looking at the cross and saying:
Look what Jesus did.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your private life in a Facebook comment section. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone scrolling beneath you may need to discover that Christians are not people who never needed rescue.
We are people who know the Rescuer.
Not because every sentence will be easy to revisit, but because someday temptation may begin making an old boundary look negotiable again.
Not as proof that you are better than the Herods of the world.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of using what God has entrusted to you for the spread of biblical truth. Jesus already paid the price of redemption in full.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend whose faith is barely breathing.
Invite the believer who has become lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Invite the person who thinks their past has disqualified them forever.
Because perhaps they do not need another polished religious performance.
Perhaps they need someone brave enough to tell them:
Yes, sin is real.
Yes, God's boundaries matter.
Yes, repentance may cost you something.
But no...
your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still mercy for the repentant.
There is still cleansing for the stained.
There is still restoration for the broken.
There is still Jesus.
And maybe the sentence you need to carry with you after everything else fades is this:
The secret you thought would become the last sentence of your life may become the very place where Jesus begins writing grace in the margins.
